title: 1mind vs Knock AI vs Storylane RepX: 2026 Buyer Guide
summary: 1mind vs Knock AI compared on pricing, setup, and engagement, plus where Storylane RepX wins when the conversion moment is an interactive demo.
body_markdown:
I run marketing at Storylane, so read this knowing I have a horse in the race. My honest read on **1mind vs Knock AI** is that most comparison pages get the question wrong, arguing over which AI sales agent is "better" when the two tools are built for different jobs. The real decision is which shape fits your buyer's motion, and if that motion is self-serve interactive demos, a third option belongs in the room.


> **Definition:** An AI sales agent is software that engages website visitors or inbound leads in a human-like conversation to answer questions, run product demos, qualify intent, and route or book meetings, without a live rep in the room for the first touch.


Here is the argument I am going to defend: 1mind and Knock AI both do real work, but neither is demo-native. The buyers I talk to keep saying their number-one problem is letting prospects evaluate the product without a sales call. That is a demo problem first and a chat problem second.


## TL;DR: the 30-second verdict on 1mind vs Knock AI


Short on time? Here is the whole comparison compressed into four lines, with the honest caveat that these three tools are optimized for different buyer motions rather than competing head-on for the same job.


- **1mind** is a premium, avatar-led on-site sales agent. Strong if you want a "Superhuman" rep persona that greets, demos, and handles objections, and you can absorb a six-figure contract and a one-to-two-month rollout.
- **Knock AI** is a buyer-engagement platform that captures and converts demand across web plus messaging channels. Strong if your gap is multichannel follow-up and fast time-to-value, and you trust vendor-reported outcome numbers until you verify them.
- **Storylane RepX** is an interactive-demo-native agent. Strong if the core job is letting buyers test-drive the product and self-serve answers on your site, then handing clean intent to your CRM.
- **Who wins for whom:** pick 1mind for a high-touch avatar experience, Knock AI for multichannel demand capture, and RepX when the conversion moment is an interactive demo.

If you want a broader field before you commit, we also keep a running list of the[best AI SDR tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/top-ai-sdr-tools) , and a related[compare demo platforms](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demostack-vs-walnut-a-comparison-of-its-features-and-pricing) breakdown.

Treat every "vendor-reported" cell as a claim to verify in your own trial, not a settled fact. That skepticism is the whole point of this piece.


## What each platform actually does


The category label "AI sales agent" hides big differences in where and how each tool engages. Before you compare features, get clear on the core motion each product is designed around. That single distinction predicts most of your day-two experience.


### 1mind in one paragraph


1mind sells "Superhuman" AI sales agents: an on-site, avatar-led persona that greets visitors, delivers a guided demo, handles objections, and qualifies in real time. The experience leans on a realistic video avatar as the centerpiece of the interaction. It is the most theatrical option here, and for some brands that presence is exactly the draw.


### Knock AI in one paragraph


Knock AI is a B2B buyer-engagement platform that captures and converts demand across the website plus messaging surfaces like LinkedIn, Slack, WhatsApp, and email. Its pitch is breadth of touchpoints and speed to live, so intent gets worked wherever the buyer already is. It is less about a single on-site persona and more about a connected demand-capture net.


### Storylane RepX in one paragraph


RepX is Storylane's AI sales agent built around interactive demos rather than avatars or pure chat. It lets a visitor test-drive the actual product on your site, answers questions in context, qualifies, and passes intent to your CRM. The wedge is simple: the conversion moment is the demo, and RepX is[demo automation](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-automation) first.


## Pricing compared: 1mind vs Knock AI


Start with the number everyone circles. 1mind runs at the top of the market, and its own leadership has said so publicly.


Vendor Public pricing What to expect


1mind Not listed; six-figure Six-figure average annual contract, no public rate card (TechCrunch, 2025)


Knock AI Not listed Quote-based; request a scoped proposal


Storylane RepX Not listed Plan-based; contact Storylane for a quote


1mind's pricing is the recurring hook across every ranking page, and for good reason: a six-figure commitment changes who can even evaluate it. Its own leadership has confirmed on record that contracts run in the six figures annually, with no public rate card (TechCrunch, 2025). That is not a knock on the product, it is a filter: if your annual tooling budget for this category is smaller, 1mind is out before the demo starts.


Knock AI does not publish list pricing either, and no buyer on our calls stated a clean, attributable Knock figure, so treat any number you see elsewhere as unverified. The pattern across this whole category is opacity, which puts the burden on you to force clarity in the room. Ask for a written scope, a per-outcome breakdown, and a term that ties spend to activation rather than signature.


My rule after sitting through dozens of these cycles: never accept an undisclosed six-figure quote without knowing exactly what triggers the invoice. Get the ramp, the seat or usage model, and the renewal uplift in writing. A vendor confident in its value will put activation milestones in the contract; one that resists is telling you something.


## Deployment and time-to-value


Speed to live is the second wedge in this comparison, and it maps to how each tool is architected. An avatar experience with heavy configuration takes longer to stand up than a templated demo or a messaging connector. That gap shows up in your first quarter, not your first call.


> **Timeline reality check:** 1mind reports a 1-to-2-month setup (1mind, 2026). Knock AI reports 1-to-3-day setup (Knock AI, vendor-reported, 2026). RepX deploys in days because the demo, not a bespoke avatar, is the payload.


The buyers most sensitive to this are the ones already mid-switch. As one put it plainly:


> "I guess creation of demos need to be really fast as my number one criteria right now just because we're moving off of the solution." - \[Senior Director of Product Marketing, B2B martech/ABM software\]


If you are replacing an incumbent under a deadline, weigh time-to-value as heavily as feature depth. A tool you cannot launch this quarter is not really in the running.


## Engagement model: proactive on-site vs multichannel demand capture


This is where 1mind and Knock AI genuinely diverge, and where most pages stay vague. The question is not "does it have AI chat," it is where and to whom the agent engages.


- **1mind:** proactive, on-site, avatar-first. It intercepts visitors and runs a live persona experience in the browser.
- **Knock AI:** multichannel. It works demand across web plus LinkedIn, Slack, WhatsApp, and email, meeting buyers on the channel they already use.
- **Storylane RepX:** on-site and demo-led, with targeting so the agent engages the right visitors instead of everyone.


Targeting matters more than vendors admit. Buyers told us a large share of homepage traffic is existing customers who should not be served a sales prompt at all. One flatly preferred a human handoff for engaged prospects:


> "We prefer if we're connecting with them then we're just having a conversation with AE or BDR directly on the phone." - \[role not captured, construction tech\]


So the honest engagement question is not "AI on every visitor." It is whether the tool can tell a net-new prospect from a logged-in customer, and route each correctly. If you sell demand generation as part of the motion, read this alongside how a[digital sales room software](https://www.storylane.io/blog/digital-sales-room-software) approach frames buyer engagement.


## Feature-by-feature


Coverage is table stakes; the differences live in the details. I have split this into the four areas buyers actually poke at during evaluations.


### Website engagement and qualification


All three tools engage and qualify on the site, but the qualifying mechanism differs. 1mind qualifies through avatar conversation, Knock AI through multichannel prompts, and RepX through what a visitor does inside a live demo. Demo behavior is a stronger intent signal than a chat reply, because it shows the buyer evaluating the actual product. If you want to sharpen how the agent should[qualify and run discovery](https://www.storylane.io/blog/discovery-call-agenda) , the demo path gives you richer signals to score.


### Post-session and email follow-up


Few comparison pages cover what happens after the visitor leaves, which is exactly where deals leak. Knock AI's strength is multichannel follow-up, while 1mind's is more on-session and avatar-led. The buyer test is whether captured intent, including topic-level detail, lands cleanly in your CRM so a rep can act on it, which is why RepX passes intent and topics into HubSpot or Salesforce.


### Ride-Along on live calls


Credit where it is due: 1mind launched Ride-Along around May 2026 (1mind, 2026), letting its AI join live calls, and it is a genuine strength rarely covered fairly. If your reps want an AI copilot present during human conversations, that is a real point in 1mind's favor. RepX takes a different stance, running the self-serve demo motion before the call so the human conversation starts with a qualified, product-educated buyer, and neither approach is universally better.


### CRM and Salesforce-native integration and attribution


Attribution is where "interesting demo" becomes "sourced pipeline." All three connect to CRM, but native depth and the cleanliness of the intent payload vary. RepX is CRM-native with HubSpot and Salesforce and hands over intent and topic properties, so engagement becomes attributable pipeline rather than an unlabeled activity log. Ask each vendor to show you a real record post-session, not a slide.


## Security and compliance


Enterprise buyers gate on procurement and legal, so compliance posture can decide the deal before features do. Here is where each stands on the badges that matter.


- **1mind:** SOC 2 Type II and GDPR / EU-US Data Privacy Framework (1mind Trust Center, 2025); ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 are vendor-reported, and HIPAA status is unconfirmed at time of writing.
- **Knock AI:** verify current certifications directly with the vendor; treat any uncited claim as unconfirmed.
- **Storylane RepX:** SOC 2 Type II and GDPR compliant (Storylane Trust Center, 2025), with data-handling controls for enterprise review.


Beyond badges, enterprise legal will want to redline at the package level and understand how liability is handled, and some buyers require region-specific hosting such as EU-based infrastructure. Do not save this for the last week. Put security review, redline flexibility, and data-residency questions in your first vendor conversation, because a tool that cannot pass legal is not a shortlist item no matter how good the demo looks. Ask each vendor for its current attestation letters, not a badge on a marketing page, and confirm the certification is in effect rather than in progress. If your buyers span regulated industries or the EU, get the hosting region and data-processing terms in writing before you invest evaluation time.


## Which one is right for you?


No ranking page will give you an even-handed verdict, so here is mine, drawn from what buyers actually weigh. The pressure they describe is real: a near-term deadline, a need to understand cost differences between two tools, and a need to defend one choice to procurement.


> **Best for 1mind:** brands that want a high-touch, avatar-led on-site experience as a differentiator, have budget for a six-figure contract, and can wait one to two months to go live.


> **Best for Knock AI:** teams whose gap is multichannel demand capture and follow-up, who value fast time-to-value, and who will verify vendor-reported outcomes in a scoped trial.


> **Best for Storylane RepX:** teams whose conversion moment is an interactive demo, who need buyers to self-serve answers without talking to sales, and who want clean intent flowing to CRM.


A simple decision path:


1. Is your core conversion moment an interactive product demo? If yes, start with RepX.
2. Is your gap breadth of channels and speed to live? If yes, look hard at Knock AI.
3. Do you specifically want an avatar persona and have the budget and runway? If yes, 1mind earns the look.


If pipeline shape is your real question, work backward from the funnel; our take on how to[build a pipeline funnel](https://www.storylane.io/blog/perfect-abm-funnel) pairs well with this decision.


## Where Storylane RepX fits (full disclosure: this is us)


Full disclosure: this is us, so here is the mechanism, not the marketing. RepX is built on Storylane's interactive demos, so the agent's job is to put the working product in front of a buyer and let them evaluate it, then capture what they engaged with and push it to CRM. That matters because the strongest signal I hear from buyers is a demo problem, not a chat problem.


> "With 1Mind you don't get interactive demos that you can show." - \[Director of Presales Operations, HR/workforce software\]


Two worked examples show where this fits, and in both the demo is the unit of work. First, field-sales enablement: a technical founder described handing in-person sellers a link to an on-site Storylane assistant preloaded with demo steps and a product presentation, so the demo travels with the rep. Second, website demand generation: a buyer with little existing online demand wanted the agent to build demand and then convert it with self-serve interactivity.


Where RepX does not fit: if you want a talking avatar as a brand statement, that is not our bet, and 1mind will feel more on-theme. And if your motion is genuinely multichannel outbound across Slack and WhatsApp, Knock AI's spread is wider than ours. I would rather tell you that than pretend RepX is everything.


## What real users say


Independent review signal is thin and uneven across this matchup, so weigh it carefully rather than treat it as a scoreboard. Knock AI shows strong sentiment on G2 at 4.9 out of 5 across 22 reviews (G2, 2026). That is a small sample, which is common in an emerging category, so read the review text, not just the star average.


For 1mind, the most useful "review" signal I have is what buyers say when they compare it to an interactive-demo approach. The recurring theme is the demo gap named above, and it shows up again when buyers describe the state they are escaping:


> "We just have loose demos floating in our sales instance for the sales team. The tracking and metrics, we're not really doing that stuff yet." - \[Senior Director of Product Marketing, B2B martech/ABM software\]


My rule for review reading in this category: discount raw star averages under 50 reviews, and instead look for whether reviewers describe your specific use case. A 4.9 from a use case unlike yours is weaker evidence than a 4.2 from a team that looks exactly like you.


## How we would evaluate any AI sales agent (buyer checklist)


No vendor page hands you a reusable scorecard, so take this one and apply it beyond these three tools. Score each vendor one to five on every line, then weight to your motion.


1. **Conversion moment:** does the agent's core action match your real conversion event, whether that is a demo, a chat, or a booked meeting?
2. **Audience targeting:** can it tell a net-new prospect from a logged-in customer and route each correctly?
3. **Time-to-value:** can you launch it this quarter, or does rollout stretch into months?
4. **Intent handoff:** does topic-level intent land cleanly in your CRM for rep follow-up?
5. **Follow-up reach:** does it work leads on the channels your buyers actually use?
6. **Pricing transparency:** is spend tied to activation and outcomes, or just to signature?
7. **Compliance fit:** does it clear SOC 2, region-specific hosting, and legal redlines without a fire drill?
8. **Outcome proof:** can the vendor show a real customer record, not a vendor-reported average?


Run all three tools through this before a single pricing call. The scorecard, not the sales deck, is what defends your choice to procurement.


## Frequently asked questions


**Is 1mind or Knock AI cheaper?**


Knock AI is likely more accessible on price, though neither publishes public list pricing. 1mind is openly six-figure, running as an enterprise, annual contract with no public rate card (TechCrunch, 2025). Always get a written, outcome-tied scope before comparing quotes.


**How long does each take to deploy?**


1mind reports a one-to-two-month setup, reflecting its avatar-heavy configuration (1mind, 2026). Knock AI reports a one-to-three-day setup (Knock AI, vendor-reported, 2026). If speed to live matters, weigh it as heavily as features, especially if you are replacing an incumbent under a deadline.


**What is the difference between 1mind and Knock AI's engagement model?**


1mind is a proactive on-site avatar that engages visitors in the browser. Knock AI is multichannel, working demand across web plus LinkedIn, Slack, WhatsApp, and email. The right pick depends on whether your buyers convert on-site or across many channels.


**Where does Storylane RepX fit in this comparison?**


RepX is the interactive-demo-native option: it lets buyers test-drive the product on your site, qualifies from real demo behavior, and hands intent to CRM. Choose it when the conversion moment is a demo rather than an avatar chat or a multichannel sequence.


**Are Knock AI's outcome numbers trustworthy?**


They are vendor-reported, so treat figures like faster cycles or higher reply rates as claims to verify, not settled facts. Ask for a live customer record and reproduce the result in a scoped trial before you rely on it.


## The bottom line on 1mind vs Knock AI


The 1mind vs Knock AI debate is really three questions wearing one keyword: do you want an avatar, multichannel reach, or a demo? 1mind wins on avatar presence and its new Ride-Along on live calls, Knock AI wins on channel breadth and speed to live, and Storylane RepX wins when the buyer's job is to self-serve an interactive demo and convert on your site. Match the tool to your conversion moment, verify every vendor-reported number in a trial, and defend the choice with the scorecard above.


The 1mind vs Knock AI question stops being hard the moment you name your own conversion event honestly. An avatar that dazzles in a sales call still has to earn attribution in your CRM and clear your legal review, so weight the boring criteria as heavily as the exciting ones. Pick the tool your buyers will actually convert through, then hold the vendor to the scorecard rather than the pitch.
